<a id="doc-120-slack"></a>

## [120] Slack

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations
- **출처 (URL)**: [https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/slack](https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/slack)

On this page

# Slack

The **Timbr chat bot** lets your team ask questions about your data in plain English from Slack. Every answer is computed by your own Timbr instance, under the asking user's own permissions — the same engine behind [Ask Timbr](</doc/docs/platform/ask-timbr>), surfaced in the tool your team already has open.

## How it works​

The chat bot is **not a separate service**. It runs inside the Timbr API service as a blueprint mounted at `/timbr/api/chatbot/*` and executes each query in-process.

  1. **Slack** delivers the message over an HTTPS webhook — a direct message, an `@AskTimbr` mention, a slash command or a button click. There is no Socket Mode, no polling and no outbound connection to maintain.
  2. **The Timbr API service** verifies the request signature, resolves the asking user's verified email address, generates semantic SQL for the question and runs it.
  3. **Your data** is queried through your ontology, impersonating the asker via the `platform` credential the API service already holds.



Because there is no shared identity and no service-account token, you get **per-user permissions and per-user audit trails** — nobody can see through the bot anything they could not see in the platform.

## What your team gets​

Where| What to type| Notes  
---|---|---  
Slack direct message| `<question>`| No mention or command needed in a DM.  
Slack channel| `@AskTimbr <question>`| The bot must be in the channel. Replies in a thread.  
Slack, anywhere| `/asktimbr <question>`| Works without inviting the bot to the channel.  
Anywhere| `help`| `?` works too. Lists every surface and override.  
  
**Quick commands** are answered immediately, without calling the LLM: `list ontologies`, `list agents`, `list concepts`, `list views` and `list cubes`.

**Override the default source** by prefixing any question. This works on every surface:
    
    
    ontology:sales_data  How many leads?  
    agent:my_agent       What is total revenue?  
    

**Every answer carries follow-up buttons** — _Show SQL_ , _Show Result Set_ and _Export CSV_ — so an analyst can verify the query that produced the number. In a channel those follow-ups are ephemeral: only the person who asked sees them.

## Requirements​

The bot is configured on your existing Timbr API service instance, not on a new server:

Requirement| Details  
---|---  
**Turned on**| `ENABLE_CHAT_BOT=true`, plus one of `CHAT_BOT_DEFAULT_ONTOLOGY` or `CHAT_BOT_DEFAULT_AGENT`  
**A public HTTPS endpoint**|  Webhooks are delivered to it by Slack, so it must be reachable from the internet and present a valid certificate  
**LLM configuration**| `TIMBR_LLM_TYPE`, `TIMBR_LLM_MODEL`, `TIMBR_LLM_APIKEY` — the natural language to SQL call is made by the API service itself  
**Redis**|  Backs result state, the identity cache, event de-duplication and the in-flight guard. Required for correctness whenever more than one worker is running  
  
## Setup​

Slack installation is driven by a pre-built app manifest, so there is nothing to fill in by hand in the Slack UI.

The interactive walkthrough for Slack is still being finalised. Until it is published, contact Timbr support for the Slack app manifest and the installation steps.

<a id="doc-121-snowflake"></a>

## [121] Snowflake

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations
- **출처 (URL)**: [https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/datasources/snowflake/overview](https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/datasources/snowflake/overview)

On this page

# Snowflake

Snowflake is a cloud-based data warehousing platform that offers a unique architecture separating compute and storage. It provides scalability, concurrent access, and robust performance for data analytics workloads.

Timbr + Snowflake Logo

Integrating Snowflake with Timbr combines the strengths of both platforms. It allows you to use Timbr's semantic graph capabilities alongside Snowflake's powerful cloud data warehousing features. This integration enhances your ability to perform semantic querying, data virtualization, and integrated data management in a scalable cloud environment, leading to faster insights and more efficient data operations.

## Getting Started with Snowflake​

If you haven't yet connected to a Snowflake account, follow these steps to set up and establish a connection:

  * [Snowflake Documentation](<https://docs.snowflake.com/>)
  * [Snowflake Getting Started](<https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide-getting-started>)
  * [Support](<https://community.snowflake.com/s/>)



To connect Timbr to your Snowflake datasource, you need to use the Snowflake JDBC driver. For information on the Snowflake JDBC driver and how to set it up, refer to the [Snowflake JDBC Driver documentation](<https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/jdbc>).

## Connecting Timbr to Snowflake in the Timbr Platform​

Once you've set up a Snowflake account and have the JDBC driver ready, it's time to connect Timbr to Snowflake. Follow the steps below for a detailed tutorial on connecting Timbr to Snowflake:

  1. **Navigate to Manage Datasources** : From the Timbr interface, click on the **Manage tab** and select **Datasources**.

  2. **Add New Datasource** : On the top right, click the **Add New Datasource** button. Alternatively, you can click the big add button beneath the knowledge graphs and datasources tabs.




Add new datasource

  3. **Fill in Connection Details** : A pop-up window will appear where you need to provide the relevant connection details to connect Snowflake to Timbr.



There are two options in Timbr to enter the connection information: **Simple** or **JDBC Url**.

On the top right of the pop-up window , the toggle can be switched from _Simple_ to _JDBC Url_ in order to connect the datasource using the relevant JDBC URL.

tabs

#### Simple Tab Connection Configuration​

  1. **Select Simple Tab** : Ensure the Simple tab is selected.

  2. **Fill in the Following Details** :

     * **Database Type** : Select Snowflake.
     * **Datasource Name** : Enter a name for your datasource.
     * **Description** : Provide a description of the datasource (Optional).
     * **Hostname / IP** : Enter the hostname or IP address of your Snowflake datasource.
     * **Username** : Enter your Snowflake username.
     * **Password** : Enter your Snowflake password.
     * **Additional Parameters** : Add any additional connection parameters using `&` as separators.



#### JDBC URL Tab Configuration​

  1. **Select JDBC URL Tab** : Ensure the JDBC URL tab is selected.

  2. **Fill in the Following Details** :

     * **Database Type** : Select Snowflake.
     * **Datasource Name** : Enter a name for your datasource.
     * **Description** : Provide a description of the datasource (Optional).
     * **Username** : Enter your Snowflake username.
     * **Password** : Enter your Snowflake password.
     * **JDBC URL** : Enter the JDBC connection URL (e.g., `jdbc:snowflake://[host]/`).



jdbc tab

#### Save and Test Connection​

  1. After entering the details, click the **Save** button to save the information, connecting the Snowflake datasource to the Timbr environment.
  2. Once saved, on the top right, click the **Test connection** button to verify the datasource’s connectivity, ensuring it is active and responsive.



For a comprehensive guide on connecting Timbr to various datasources, refer to the detailed documentation:

  * [Connecting Timbr to Datasources](<https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/platform/managing/datasource-manager>)

# Tableau

## Connecting Tableau to the Timbr Knowledge Graph​

  1. Open **Tableau**



In the main window under **Connect** go to the **To a Server** list and click on **More..**.

image

**Please make sure to download and install the latest ODBC driver from here:** <https://www.databricks.com/spark/odbc-drivers-download>

  2. Fill in the following details:



> Connection: **SparkThriftServer (Spark 1.1 and later)**
> 
> Server: **timbr-server IP or HOSTNAME**
> 
> Port: **timbr-server port** (default **11000**)
> 
> Authentication: **Username and Password**
> 
> Username: **token@\ <ontology_name>**
> 
> Password: **\ <user_token>**
> 
> Transport: **HTTP**
> 
> HTTP Path: Leave empty **(when routing is enabled the path should be hive2 or timbr-server)**
> 
> Require SSL: **false** by default, **true** If SSL is enabled (using gateway or load-balancer)

  3. **Loading Schemas & Tables:**



**Option #1** \- Loading from a specific concept:

Once the connection is successful, click on **Select Schema** and write the schema you want to load (timbr/dtimbr/vtimbr).

After that click add (**+**) - make sure the **Exact** option is selected.

image

Once found, either click on **Load** or in some cases the concept list will appear automatically.

image

Once loaded, drag the concept you want to visualize and go to the **Sheet 1** button (on the bottom-left side) to start visualizing.

image

**Option #2** \- Using a Custom SQL query:

After loading the desired schema, click on **New Custom SQL**.

image

Enter the custom query:

image

Click on **OK** and go to worksheet to visualize the results.

image

Congrats! You're ready to use the concepts and their relationships for your visualizations!

<a id="doc-123-timbr-jdbc-connector"></a>

## [123] Timbr JDBC Connector

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations
- **출처 (URL)**: [https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/python/python_jdbc](https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/python/python_jdbc)

On this page

# Timbr JDBC Connector

This is a sample for connecting to Timbr using JDBC and Python.

## Dependencies​

  * Access to a **Timbr Server** service
  * Python version `3.9.13` or newer
  * Java `11` / Java `17` / Java `21`



## Installation​

  * Install as clone repository:

    * Install Python: <https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3913/>
    * Install Java: <https://www.oracle.com/il-en/java/technologies/javase/jdk11-archive-downloads.html>
    * Run the following command to install the Python dependencies: `pip install -r requirements.txt` (optional install pandas to run pandas example)
    * Download the following jar to `jars` path: <https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/apache/hive/hive-jdbc/4.0.1/hive-jdbc-4.0.1-standalone.jar>
  * Install using pip and git: `pip install git+https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_connector`

  * Install using pip: `pip install pytimbr`




## Sample usage​

  * For an example of how to use the Python connector for Timbr:
    * Create connection with params, follow this [Example file](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_connector/blob/main/examples/example.py>)
    * Create JDBC connection, follow this [Example file](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_connector/blob/main/examples/example_JDBC.py>)
  * For an example of using the Timbr Python connector with Pandas:
    * Make sure you have the pandas library installed, or you can install it by running `pip install pandas`
    * Create connection with params, follow this [Example File](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_connector/blob/main/examples/pandas_example.py>)
    * Create JDBC connection, follow this [Example File](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_connector/blob/main/examples/pandas_example_JDBC.py>)



## Connection parameters examples​

### Parameters for basic connection​

#### Generic example and explanation for each parameter​
    
    
      hostname = '<TIMBR_IP/HOST>'  
      port = '<TIMBR_PORT>'  
      ontology = '<ONTOLOGY_NAME>'  
      username = '<token/TIMBR_USER>'  
      password = '<TOKEN_VALUE/TIMBR_PASSWORD>'  
      enabled_ssl = '<false/true>'  
      http_path = '<TIMBR_SERVER_HTTP_PATH>'  
        
      # hostname    - Required  - String  - The IP / Hostname of the Timbr server (not necessarily the hostname of the Timbr platform).  
      # port        - Required  - String  - The port to connect to in the Timbr server. Timbr's default port with enabled_ssl is 443 without SSL is 11000.  
      # ontology    - Required  - String  - the ontology / knowledge graph to connect to.  
      # username    - Required  - String  - Use 'token' as the username when connecting using a Timbr token, otherwise its the user name.  
      # password    - Required  - String  - Should be the token value if using a token as a username, otherwise its the user's password.  
      # enabled_ssl - Optional  - String  - 'true' if SSL is enabled, 'false' if SSL is disabled. The default value is 'true'.  
      # http_path   - Optional  - String  - Use only if your timbr server http path is not '/timbr-server'. The default value is '/timbr-server'.  
    

#### HTTP example​
    
    
      hostname = 'mytimbrenv.com'  
      port = '11000'  
      ontology = 'my_ontology'  
      username = 'timbr'  
      password = 'StrongPassword'  
      enabled_ssl = 'false'  
      http_path = '/timbr-server'  
    

#### HTTPS example​
    
    
      hostname = 'mytimbrenv.com'  
      port = '443'  
      ontology = 'my_ontology'  
      username = 'timbr'  
      password = 'StrongPassword'  
      enabled_ssl = 'true'  
      http_path = '/timbr-server'  
    

### Parameters for JDBC connection​

#### Generic example and explanation for each parameter​
    
    
      jdbc_url = '<TIMBR_JDBC_CONNECTION_URL>'  
      username = '<token/TIMBR_USER>'  
      password = '<TOKEN_VALUE/TIMBR_PASSWORD>'  
      
      # jdbc_url  - Required  - String  - The JDBC connection url.  
      # username  - Required  - String  - Use 'token' as the username when connecting using a Timbr token, otherwise its the user name.  
      # password  - Required  - String  - Should be the token value if using a token as a username, otherwise its the user's password.  
    

#### HTTP example​
    
    
      jdbc_url = 'jdbc:hive2://mytimbrenv.com:11000/my_ontology;transportMode=http;ssl=false;httpPath=/timbr-server'  
      username = 'timbr'  
      password = 'StrongPassword'  
    

#### HTTPS example​
    
    
      jdbc_url = 'jdbc:hive2://mytimbrenv.com:443/my_ontology;transportMode=http;ssl=true;httpPath=/timbr-server'  
      username = 'timbr'  
      password = 'StrongPassword'  
    

## Create new connection​

### Create a basic connection​

#### Generic example​
    
    
      conn = pytimbr.get_connection(  
        hostname,  
        port,  
        ontology,  
        username,  
        password,  
        enabled_ssl,  
        http_path  
      )  
    

#### HTTP example​
    
    
      conn = pytimbr.get_connection(  
        'mytimbrenv.com',  
        '11000',  
        'my_ontology',  
        'timbr',  
        'StrongPassword',  
        'false',  
        '/timbr-server'  
      )  
    

#### HTTPS example​
    
    
      hostname = 'mytimbrenv.com'  
      port = '443'  
      ontology = 'my_ontology'  
      username = 'timbr'  
      password = 'StrongPassword'  
      enabled_ssl = 'true'  
      http_path = '/timbr-server'  
    

### Create a JDBC connection​

#### Generic example​
    
    
      conn = pytimbr.get_jdbc_connection(  
        jdbc_url,  
        username,  
        password  
      )  
    

#### HTTP example​
    
    
      conn = pytimbr.get_jdbc_connection(  
        "jdbc:hive2://mytimbrenv.com:11000/my_ontology;transportMode=http;ssl=false;httpPath=/timbr-server",  
        'timbr',  
        'StrongPassword'  
      )  
    

#### HTTPS example​
    
    
      conn = pytimbr.get_jdbc_connection(  
        "jdbc:hive2://mytimbrenv.com:443/my_ontology;transportMode=http;ssl=true;httpPath=/timbr-server",  
        'timbr',  
        'StrongPassword'  
      )  
    

## Execute a query​
    
    
      # Use the connection to execute a query  
      with conn.cursor() as curs:  
        # Execute query  
        curs.execute('SHOW CONCEPTS')  
      
        # Fetch results  
        concepts = curs.fetchall()  
      
        # Print returned object headers  
        # Option 1 - Recommended  
        for i in range(1, curs._meta.getColumnCount() + 1):  
          print(curs._meta.getColumnName(i) + " - " + curs._meta.getColumnTypeName(i))  
      
        # Option 2- DBAPI  
        for col in curs.description:  
          print(col[0] + " - " + col[1].values[0])  
      
        # Print the results  
        for concept in concepts:  
          print(concept)  
    

### Execute a query using `Pandas`​
    
    
      import pandas  
      # Execute a query using Pandas  
      df = pandas.read_sql("SELECT * FROM timbr.person limit 1000", conn)  
      print("--------------------------------------")  
      print(df)  
      print("--------------------------------------")  
      print(df.columns)  
      print("--------------------------------------")  
      print(df.count())

## [124] Timbr REST API Connector

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations
- **출처 (URL)**: [https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/python/python_http](https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/python/python_http)

On this page

# Timbr REST API Connector

This sample is of a pure Python connector to Timbr without any dependencies required.

## Dependencies​

  * Access to a **Timbr Server** service
  * Python version `3.9.13` or newer



## Installation​

  * Install as clone repository:

    * Install Python: <https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3913/>
  * Install using pip and git: `pip install git+https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_http`

  * Install using pip: `pip install pytimbr-api`




## Sample usage​

  * For an example of how to use the REST API connector for Timbr, follow this [Example file](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_http/blob/main/examples/example.py>)



## Connection parameters examples​

### Generic example and explanation for each parameter​
    
    
      pytimbr_api.run_query(  
        url = "<TIMBR_URL>",  
        ontology = "<ONTOLOGY_NAME>",  
        token = "<USER_TOKEN>",  
        query = "<TIMBR_QUERY>",  
        datasource = "<DATASOURCE_NAME>",  
        nested = "<true/false>",  
        verify_ssl = <True/False>,  
        enable_IPv6 = <True/False>,  
      )  
      
      # url           - Required - String - The IP / Hostname of the Timbr platform.  
      # ontology      - Required - String - The ontology / knowledge graph to connect to.  
      # token         - Required - String - Timbr token value or JWT token value. Note: If you are using JWT token, you need to set the is_jwt parameter to True.  
      # query         - Required - String - The query that you want to execute.  
      # datasource    - Optional - String - Add the specific datasource name that you want to query from, the default value is the current active datasource of your ontology.  
      # nested        - Optional - String - Change to 'true' if nested flag needs to be enabled. make sure this flag contains string value not bool value.  
      # verify_ssl    - Optional - Boolean - Verifying the target server's SSL Certificate, use False to disable this process.  
      # enable_IPv6   - Optional - Boolean - Change to 'true' if you are using IPv6 connection.  
      # is_jwt        - Optional - Boolean - Set to True if you are using JWT token, otherwise set to False.  
      # jwt_tenant_id - Optional - String - The tenant ID for JWT authentication  
    

### Using Timbr Token​

#### HTTP Example​
    
    
      pytimbr_api.run_query(  
        url = "http://mytimbrenv.com:11000",  
        ontology = "my_ontology",  
        token = "tk_mytimbrtoken",  
        query = "SELECT * FROM timbr.sys_concepts",  
        datasource = "my_datasource",  
        nested = "false",  
        verify_ssl = False,  
        enable_IPv6 = False,  
      )  
    

#### HTTPS Example​
    
    
      pytimbr_api.run_query(  
        url = "https://mytimbrenv.com:443",  
        ontology = "my_ontology",  
        token = "tk_mytimbrtoken",  
        query = "SELECT * FROM timbr.sys_concepts",  
        datasource = "my_datasource",  
        nested = "false",  
        verify_ssl = True,  
        enable_IPv6 = False,  
      )  
    

### Using JWT​

#### HTTP Example​
    
    
      pytimbr_api.run_query(  
        url = "http://mytimbrenv.com:11000",  
        ontology = "my_ontology",  
        token = "tk_mytimbrtoken",  
        query = "SELECT * FROM timbr.sys_concepts",  
        datasource = "my_datasource",  
        nested = "false",  
        verify_ssl = False,  
        enable_IPv6 = False,  
        is_jwt = True,  
        jwt_tenant_id = "my_tenant_id",  
      )  
    

#### HTTPS Example​
    
    
      pytimbr_api.run_query(  
        url = "https://mytimbrenv.com:11000",  
        ontology = "my_ontology",  
        token = "tk_mytimbrtoken",  
        query = "SELECT * FROM timbr.sys_concepts",  
        datasource = "my_datasource",  
        nested = "false",  
        verify_ssl = True,  
        enable_IPv6 = False,  
        is_jwt = True,  
        jwt_tenant_id = "my_tenant_id",  
      )  
    

## Execute Query Examples​

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations

On this page

# Timbr SQLAlchemy Connector

This is a sample connector to Timbr using SQLAlchemy.

## Dependencies​

  * Access to a **Timbr Server** service

  * Python version `3.9.13` or newer

  * Support SQLAlchemy version `1.4.36` or newer. (version `2.x.x` or newer is currently not supported).

  * For **Linux** based machines only install those dependencies first:

    * gcc
    * heimdal-dev
    * krb5
    * python-devel
    * python-dev
    * python-all-dev
    * libsasl2-dev
  * In **Ubuntu** run 
    
        apt install gcc, heimdal-dev, krb5, python-devel, python-dev, python-all-dev, libsasl2-dev  
    




## Installation​

  * Install as clone repository:

    * Install Python: <https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3913/>

    * Run the following command to install the Python dependencies: 

`pip install -r requirements.txt`

  * Install using pip and git:

`pip install git+https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_SQLAlchemy`

  * Install using pip:

`pip install pytimbr-sqla`




## Sample usage​

  * For an example of how to use the Python SQLAlchemy connector for timbr, follow this [example file](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_SQLAlchemy/blob/main/examples/example.py>)
  * For an example of how to use the Python SQLAlchemy connector with 'PyHive' as async query for timbr, follow this [example file](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_SQLAlchemy/blob/main/examples/pyhive_async_example.py>)
  * For an example of how to use the Python SQLAlchemy connector with 'PyHive' as sync query for timbr, follow this [example file](<https://github.com/WPSemantix/timbr_python_SQLAlchemy/blob/main/examples/pyhive_sync_example.py>)



## Connection parameters​

### General example​
    
    
      hostname = '<TIMBR_IP/HOST>'  
      port = '<TIMBR_PORT>'  
      ontology = '<ONTOLOGY_NAME>'  
      protocol = '<http/https>'  
      username = '<TIMBR_USER/token>'  
      password = '<TIMBR_PASSWORD/TOKEN_VALUE>'  
      
      # hostname - The IP / Hostname of the Timbr server (not necessarily the hostname of the Timbr platform).  
      # port - The port to connect to in the Timbr server. Timbr's default port with enabled_ssl is 443 without SSL is 11000.  
      # ontology = The name of the ontology (knowledge graph) to connect.  
      # protocol - Connection protocol can be 'http' or 'https'.  
      # username - Use 'token' as the username when connecting using a Timbr token, otherwise use the user name.  
      # password - If using a token as a username then the pass is the token value, otherwise its the user's password.  
    

### HTTP example with dummy data​

#### Username and password​
    
    
      hostname = 'mytimbrenv.com'  
      port = '11000'  
      ontology = 'my_ontology'  
      protocol = 'http'  
      username = 'timbr'  
      password = 'StrongPassword'  
    

#### Timbr token​
    
    
      hostname = 'mytimbrenv.com'  
      port = '11000'  
      ontology = 'my_ontology'  
      protocol = 'http'  
      username = 'token'  
      password = '<TOKEN_VALUE>'  
    

### HTTPS example with dummy data​

#### Timbr token​
    
    
      hostname = 'mytimbrenv.com'  
      port = '443'

      protocol = 'https'  
      username = 'token'  
      password = '<TOKEN_VALUE>'  
    

## Connection options​

### 1\. Connect using `pytimbr_sqla` and `SQLAlchemy` packages​
    
    
      from sqlalchemy import create_engine  
      
      # Declare the connection variables  
      # General example  
      hostname = '<TIMBR_IP/HOST>'  
      port = '<TIMBR_PORT>'  
      ontology = '<ONTOLOGY_NAME>'  
      protocol = '<http/https>'  
      username = '<TIMBR_USER/token>'  
      password = '<TIMBR_PASSWORD/TOKEN_VALUE>'  
      
      # hostname - The IP / Hostname of the Timbr server (not necessarily the hostname of the Timbr platform).  
      # port - The port to connect to in the Timbr server. Timbr's default port with enabled_ssl is 443 without SSL is 11000.  
      # ontology = The name of the ontology (knowledge graph) to connect.  
      # protocol - Connection protocol can be 'http' or 'https'.  
      # username - Use 'token' as the username when connecting using a Timbr token, otherwise use the user name.  
      # password - If using a token as a username then the pass is the token value, otherwise its the user's password.  
      
      # Create new sqlalchemy connection  
      engine = create_engine(f"timbr+{protocol}://{username}@{ontology}:{password}@{hostname}:{port}")  
      
      # Connect to the created engine  
      conn = engine.connect()  
      
      # Execute a query  
      query = "SHOW CONCEPTS"  
      res_obj = conn.execute(query)  
      results_headers = [(desc[0], desc[1]) for desc in res_obj.cursor.description]  
      
      # Optional Performance Tuning:  
      # By default, Timbr fetches results in batches of 10,000 rows at a time.  
      # You can increase this batch size for better performance with large datasets.  
      # Note: The maximum batch size is controlled by your Timbr server's   
      # "TIMBR_RESULTSET_MAX_FETCH_SIZE" configuration setting.  
      res_obj.cursor._arraysize = 20000  
      
      results = res_obj.fetchall()  
      
      # Print the columns name  
      for name, col_type in results_headers:  
        print(f"{name} - {col_type}")  
      # Print the results  
      for result in results:  
        print(result)  
    

### 2\. Connect using `PyHive` and `SQLAlchemy` packages​

Attention

**PyHive** provides two operational modes: **asynchronous** and **synchronous**.

However, Timbr exclusively supports **asynchronous** query execution when using PyHive.

#### Connect using PyHive **Asynchronous** Mode​
    
    
      from sqlalchemy import create_engine  
      from TCLIService.ttypes import TOperationState  
      
      # Declare the connection variables  
      # General example  
      hostname = '<TIMBR_IP/HOST>'  
      port = '<TIMBR_PORT>'  
      ontology = '<ONTOLOGY_NAME>'  
      protocol = '<http/https>'  
      username = '<TIMBR_USER/token>'  
      password = '<TIMBR_PASSWORD/TOKEN_VALUE>'  
      connect_args = {  
        'configuration': {  
          'set:hiveconf:hiveMetadata': 'true',  
          'set:hiveconf:active_datasource': '<datasource_name>',  
          'set:hiveconf:queryTimeout': '<TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS>',  
        },  
      }  
      
      # hostname - The IP / Hostname of the Timbr server (not necessarily the hostname of the Timbr platform).  
      # port - The port to connect to in the Timbr server. Timbr's default port with enabled_ssl is 443 without SSL is 11000.  
      # ontology = The name of the ontology (knowledge graph) to connect.  
      # protocol - Connection protocol can be 'http' or 'https'.  
      # username - Use 'token' as the username when connecting using a Timbr token, otherwise use the user name.  
      # password - If using a token as a username then the pass is the token value, otherwise its the user's password.  
      # connect_args - The connection special arguments for extra customization. The only argument you must have is the first one (set:hiveconf:hiveMetadata) the others are optional.  
      
      # Create new sqlalchemy connection  
      engine = create_engine(f"hive+{protocol}://{username}@{ontology}:{password}@{hostname}:{port}", connect_args = connect_args)  
      
      # Connect to the created engine  
      conn = engine.connect()  
      dbapi_conn = engine.raw_connection()  
      cursor = dbapi_conn.cursor()  
      
      # Execute a query  
      query = "SHOW CONCEPTS"  
      cursor.execute(query)  
      
      # Check the status of this execution  
      status = cursor.poll().operationState  
      while status in (TOperationState.INITIALIZED_STATE, TOperationState.RUNNING_STATE):  
        status = cursor.poll().operationState  
      
      # Get the results of the execution  
      results_headers = [(desc[0], desc[1]) for desc in cursor.description]  
      results = cursor.fetchall()  
      
      # Display the results of the execution  
      # Print the columns name  
      for name, col_type in results_headers:  
        print(f"{name} - {col_type}")  
      # Print the results  
      for result in results:  
        print(result)  
    

#### Connect using PyHive **Synchronous** Mode​
    
    
      from sqlalchemy import create_engine  
      from TCLIService.ttypes import TOperationState  
      
      # Declare the connection variables  
      # General example  
      hostname = '<TIMBR_IP/HOST>'  
      port = '<TIMBR_PORT>'  
      ontology = '<ONTOLOGY_NAME>'  
      protocol = '<http/https>'  
      username = '<TIMBR_USER/token>'  
      password = '<TIMBR_PASSWORD/TOKEN_VALUE>'  
      connect_args = {  
        'configuration': {  
          'set:hiveconf:async': 'false',  
          'set:hiveconf:hiveMetadata': 'true',  
          'set:hiveconf:active_datasource': '<datasource_name>',  
          'set:hiveconf:queryTimeout': '<TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS>',  
        },  
      }  
      
      # hostname - The IP / Hostname of the Timbr server (not necessarily the hostname of the Timbr platform).  
      # port - The port to connect to in the Timbr server. Timbr's default port with enabled_ssl is 443 without SSL is 11000.  
      # ontology = The name of the ontology (knowledge graph) to connect.  
      # protocol - Connection protocol can be 'http' or 'https'.  
      # username - Use 'token' as the username when connecting using a Timbr token, otherwise use the user name.  
      # password - If using a token as a username then the pass is the token value, otherwise its the user's password.  
      # connect_args - The connection special arguments for extra customization. The only 2 arguments you must have are the first and the second one (set:hiveconf:async, set:hiveconf:hiveMetadata) the others are optional.  
      
      # Create new sqlalchemy connection  
      engine = create_engine(f"hive+{protocol}://{username}@{ontology}:{password}@{hostname}:{port}", connect_args = connect_args)  
      
      # Connect to the created engine  
      conn = engine.connect()  
      
      # Execute a query  
      query = "SHOW CONCEPTS"  
      res_obj = conn.execute(query)  
      results_headers = [(desc[0], desc[1]) for desc in res_obj.cursor.description]  
      results = res_obj.fetchall()  
      
      # Print the columns name  
      for name, col_type in results_headers:  
        print(f"{name} - {col_type}")  
      # Print the results  
      for result in results:  
        print(result)

## [126] Trino

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations

On this page

# Trino

Trino is a distributed SQL query engine designed to query large datasets across a variety of data sources. Trino supports a wide range of data formats and storage systems, providing high performance and scalability for analytics and reporting.

Timbr + Trino Logo

Integrating Trino with Timbr allows you to leverage Timbr's semantic graph capabilities while maintaining Trino's powerful query engine. This integration enables advanced features like semantic querying, data virtualization, and integrated data management, providing powerful insights and efficiencies.

## Getting Started with Trino​

If you haven't yet set up Trino, follow these steps to get started:

  * [Trino Documentation](<https://trino.io/docs/current/>)
  * [Trino Installation](<https://trino.io/docs/current/installation.html>)
  * [Support](<https://trino.io/community.html>)



To connect Timbr to your Trino datasource, you need to use the Trino JDBC driver. For information on the Trino JDBC driver and how to set it up, refer to the [Trino JDBC Driver documentation](<https://trino.io/docs/current/client/jdbc.html>).

## Connecting Timbr to Trino in the Timbr Platform​

Once you've set up Trino and have the JDBC driver ready, it's time to connect Timbr to Trino. Follow the steps below for a detailed tutorial on connecting Timbr to Trino:

  1. **Navigate to Manage Datasources** : From the Timbr interface, click on the **Manage tab** and select **Datasources**.

  2. **Add New Datasource** : On the top right, click the **Add New Datasource** button. Alternatively, you can click the big add button beneath the knowledge graphs and datasources tabs.




Add new datasource

  3. **Fill in Connection Details** : A pop-up window will appear where you need to provide the relevant connection details to connect Trino to Timbr.



There are two options in Timbr to enter the connection information: **Simple** or **JDBC Url**.

On the top right of the pop-up window , the toggle can be switched from _Simple_ to _JDBC Url_ in order to connect the datasource using the relevant JDBC URL.

tabs

#### Simple Tab Connection Configuration​

  1. **Select Simple Tab** : Ensure the Simple tab is selected.

  2. **Fill in the Following Details** :

     * **Database Type** : Select Trino.
     * **Datasource Name** : Enter a name for your datasource.
     * **Description** : Provide a description of the datasource (Optional).
     * **Hostname / IP** : Enter the hostname or IP address of the Trino database.
     * **Port** : Default is 8080.
     * **Username** : Enter your Trino username.
     * **Password** : Enter your Trino password.
     * **Database Name** : Specify the name of the database.
     * **Additional Parameters** : Add any additional connection parameters using `;`



#### JDBC URL Tab Configuration​

  1. **Select JDBC URL Tab** : Ensure the JDBC URL tab is selected.

  2. **Fill in the Following Details** :

     * **Database Type** : Select Trino.
     * **Datasource Name** : Enter a name for your datasource.
     * **Description** : Provide a description of the datasource (Optional).
     * **Username** : Enter your Trino username.
     * **Password** : Enter your Trino password.
     * **JDBC URL** : Enter the JDBC connection URL (e.g., `jdbc:trino://hostname:port`).



jdbc tab

#### Save and Test Connection​

  1. After entering the details, click the **Save** button to save the information, connecting the Trino datasource to the Timbr environment.
  2. Once saved, on the top right, click the **Test connection** button to verify the datasource’s connectivity, ensuring it is active and responsive.



For a comprehensive guide on connecting Timbr to various datasources, refer to the detailed documentation:

  * [Connecting Timbr to Datasources](<https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/platform/managing/datasource-manager>)

<a id="doc-127-usage"></a>

## [127] Usage

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations
- **출처 (URL)**: [https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/teams/usage](https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/teams/usage)

On this page

# Usage

The **AskTimbr bot** lets your team ask questions about your data in plain English from Microsoft Teams. Every answer is computed by your own Timbr instance, under the asking user's own permissions - the same engine behind [Ask Timbr](</doc/docs/platform/ask-timbr>), surfaced in the tool your team already has open.

Asking the bot a question in a Microsoft Teams personal chat

Not installed yet?

See [Install & Configure](</doc/docs/integration/teams/setup>) first.

## How it works​

The chat bot is **not a separate service**. It runs inside the Timbr API service as a blueprint mounted at `/timbr/api/chatbot/*` and executes each query in-process.

  1. **Microsoft Teams** delivers the message over an HTTPS webhook via Azure Bot Service - a direct message, an `@AskTimbr` mention, or a message extension click. There is no polling and no outbound connection to maintain.
  2. **The Timbr API service** verifies the request signature, resolves the asking user's verified email address, generates semantic SQL for the question and runs it.



Because there is no shared identity and no service-account token, you get **per-user permissions and per-user audit trails** \- nobody can see through the bot anything they could not see in the platform.

## Asking a question​

Where| What to type| Notes  
---|---|---  
Teams personal chat| `<question>`| Open the AskTimbr bot and type.  
Teams channel| `@AskTimbr <question>`| The app must be added to the team.  
Teams compose box| `…` → **Ask Timbr**|  The message extension. Teams has no global slash command.  
Anywhere| `help`| `?` works too. Lists every surface and override.  
  
An AskTimbr mention in a shared Teams conversation

## Quick commands​

Answered immediately, without calling the LLM:

Command| Returns  
---|---  
`list ontologies`| Ontologies you are allowed to query  
`list agents`| Configured agents  
`list concepts`| Concepts in the active ontology  
`list views`| Views in the active ontology  
`list cubes`| Cubes in the active ontology  
  
## Targeting a specific source​

Prefix any question to override the default configured on the server. This works on every surface:
    
    
    ontology:sales_data  How many leads?  
    agent:my_agent       What is total revenue?  
    

## Buttons under every answer​

Button| What it does  
---|---  
**Show SQL**|  The semantic SQL that produced the answer, so an analyst can verify it.  
**Show Result Set**|  A row preview, capped by `CHAT_BOT_MAX_PREVIEW_ROWS` (default 50).  
**Export CSV**|  A download link, capped by `CHAT_BOT_MAX_EXPORT_ROWS` (default 10,000).  
  
In a channel, these follow-ups are ephemeral - only the person who asked sees them.

## Troubleshooting​

**"I couldn't verify your Timbr identity"** The bot could not resolve the asker's email. Check the connector token in the Timbr API service logs, and confirm the person asking has an email address in Timbr that matches their Teams account.

For installation issues - "Invalid Bot", manifest errors, or a channel reporting as disabled - see [Install & Configure](</doc/docs/integration/teams/setup#troubleshooting>).

<a id="doc-129-visual-studio-code"></a>

## [129] Visual Studio Code

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations
- **출처 (URL)**: [https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/mcp/vscode](https://docs.timbr.ai/doc/docs/integration/mcp/vscode)

On this page

# Visual Studio Code

VS Code MCP Integration

VS Code with GitHub Copilot supports MCP servers natively. For detailed configuration instructions, visit the [official documentation](<https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/copilot-mcp>).

Setting up OAuth

Connecting with OAuth lets VS Code sign you in through your organization's identity provider automatically, using **MCP OAuth** with Dynamic Client Registration (DCR). For the full client and admin setup, follow the [OAuth Setup guide](</doc/docs/integration/mcp/authentication/oauth>).

## Connect with OAuth (Recommended)​

VS Code is a strict MCP client - it validates the server's OAuth metadata with an exact URL match, so it's important to use the full server URL, including the trailing slash.

### Add the MCP Server​

  1. Create (or edit) `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace - or run **MCP: Add Server** from the Command Palette:
    
        {  
      "servers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "type": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/"  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

No `x-api-key` header is required - VS Code triggers the OAuth flow automatically when the server responds with `401 Unauthorized`.

  2. Open the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P` / `Cmd+Shift+P`) → **MCP: List Servers** → select **timbr** → **Start Server**.

  3. VS Code discovers the OAuth endpoints automatically via Dynamic Client Registration and opens your browser so you can sign in through your organization's identity provider.

Sign in via your identity provider




Setting up OAuth

Make sure the required redirect URIs are registered with your identity provider, and that the full MCP OAuth setup is in place. Follow the [OAuth Setup guide](</doc/docs/integration/mcp/authentication/oauth>) for more information.

  4. Once connected, Timbr's tools (`query_data`, `ask_question`, `generate_sql`, `identify_concept`, and more) become available to GitHub Copilot Chat in **Agent Mode**.



Dynamic Client Registration

VS Code registers as a public OAuth client (`token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"`) using one of these redirect URIs: `http://127.0.0.1/`, `http://127.0.0.1:33418/`, `https://vscode.dev/redirect`, `https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect`. If your identity provider (e.g. Azure AD) doesn't natively support Dynamic Client Registration, your IT admin can enable it on the server by setting `MCP_OAUTH_DCR_ENABLED=true` together with `MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, and register the redirect URIs above on the identity provider app. See the [OAuth Setup guide](</doc/docs/integration/mcp/authentication/oauth>) for the complete provider configuration.

### Troubleshooting​

Error| Cause| Fix  
---|---|---  
"User did not provide client details" prompt| Dynamic Client Registration failed, so VS Code fell back to a manual client-details prompt| Enable DCR on the server (`MCP_OAUTH_DCR_ENABLED=true`), or supply the client ID/secret when prompted  
Connection fails right after the initial 401| The configured server URL doesn't exactly match the OAuth `resource` metadata (trailing slash mismatch)| Use the exact URL `https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/`, including the trailing slash  
`AADSTS50011` in browser| Redirect URI not registered on the identity provider app| Add the VS Code redirect URIs listed above to the app registration  
Nothing happens after **Start Server**|  Flow stuck at discovery| Check **Output panel → MCP: timbr** for the detailed request/response log  
  
* * *

## API Key Authentication​

If interactive sign-in isn't practical - for example on a shared machine - you can connect with a static Timbr API key instead of OAuth.

### Option 1: GitHub Copilot MCP Integration​

VS Code with GitHub Copilot supports MCP servers natively. Configure in your workspace or user settings:

#### Workspace Configuration (`.vscode/mcp.json`)​
    
    
    {  
      "servers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "type": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "${env:TIMBR_API_KEY}"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

#### With Default Agent​
    
    
    {  
      "servers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "type": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "${env:TIMBR_API_KEY}",  
            "x-agent": "agent_name"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

#### With Default Ontology​
    
    
    {  
      "servers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "type": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "${env:TIMBR_API_KEY}",  
            "x-ontology": "my_ontology"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

#### User Settings Configuration​

Add to your VS Code `settings.json`:
    
    
    {  
      "github.copilot.chat.mcp.servers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "type": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "${env:TIMBR_API_KEY}",  
            "x-ontology": "my_ontology"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

### Option 2: Generic MCP Extension​

If using a third-party MCP extension, create a configuration file as specified by the extension. Most extensions support a similar format:

#### With Agent​
    
    
    {  
      "mcpServers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "transport": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "tk_your_api_key_here",  
            "x-agent": "agent_name"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

#### With Ontology​
    
    
    {  
      "mcpServers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "transport": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "tk_your_api_key_here",  
            "x-ontology": "my_ontology"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

### Environment Variable Setup (Windows)​

Set the API key as an environment variable:
    
    
    # PowerShell (current session)  
    $env:TIMBR_API_KEY = "tk_your_api_key_here"  
      
    # PowerShell (permanent - user level)  
    [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("TIMBR_API_KEY", "tk_your_api_key_here", "User")  
    

### Environment Variable Setup (macOS/Linux)​
    
    
    # Current session  
    export TIMBR_API_KEY="tk_your_api_key_here"  
      
    # Permanent (add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc)  
    echo 'export TIMBR_API_KEY="tk_your_api_key_here"' >> ~/.zshrc

## [130] Windsurf

- **분류 (Section)**: Integrations

On this page

# Windsurf

Windsurf MCP Integration

Windsurf supports MCP servers through its settings. For detailed configuration instructions, visit the [official documentation](<https://docs.codeium.com/windsurf/mcp>).

Configure via **Settings → MCP Servers**.

## Basic Configuration​

Create or edit `~/.windsurf/mcp.json` (or use Windsurf's MCP settings UI):
    
    
    {  
      "mcpServers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "transport": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "tk_your_api_key_here"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

## With Default Agent​
    
    
    {  
      "mcpServers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "transport": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "tk_your_api_key_here",  
            "x-agent": "agent_name"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

## With Default Ontology​
    
    
    {  
      "mcpServers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "transport": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "tk_your_api_key_here",  
            "x-ontology": "my_ontology"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }  
    

## Using Environment Variables​
    
    
    {  
      "mcpServers": {  
        "timbr": {  
          "transport": "http",  
          "url": "https://<your-timbr-server>/timbr/api/mcp/",  
          "headers": {  
            "x-api-key": "${TIMBR_API_KEY}"  
          },  
          "env": {  
            "MCP_DEFAULT_ONTOLOGY": "my_ontology"  
          }  
        }  
      }  
    }
